result: Movement restraint significantly reduced swimming distance and the proportion of fast swims in zebrafish larvae at 6 and 8 dpf in both non-repeated and repeated experimental designs compared to unrestrained controls.
evaluation: Claims C1-C3 and C70-C72 provide converging evidence from multiple experimental designs (non-repeated and repeated measures) with statistically significant results (p<0.01) and visual data from Figure 1. The consistency across different experimental approaches strengthens the finding.

result: Movement restraint did not affect larval body length or swimming ability by 6 dpf, but reduced body length by 9 dpf. Prior movement restraint did not impair swimming performance when larvae were subsequently placed in unrestrained conditions.
evaluation: Claims C4-C7 demonstrate that the restraint paradigm specifically affects movement without causing general developmental impairment or lasting motor deficits by 6 dpf. Statistical support is provided (p<0.01 for body length at 9 dpf; p>0.3 for swimming measures), though the mechanism for later body length reduction remains unclear.

result: Movement restraint significantly reduced the proportion of PCNA+ proliferative cells in the forebrain (specifically in both pallium and subpallium) by 6 dpf without affecting forebrain size.
evaluation: Claims C8-C11 are well-supported by statistical analyses (p<0.01 for forebrain and pallium, p=0.01 for subpallium) and immunohistochemical data from Figure 2. The specificity to proliferative cells without affecting overall brain size suggests a targeted effect on neurogenesis rather than general growth impairment.

result: Movement restraint did not affect the proportion of PCNA+ cells in the olfactory bulb or optic tectum by 6 dpf.
evaluation: Claims C12-C13 demonstrate regional specificity of the movement-dependent neurogenic effect. Statistical support shows no significant differences (p=0.61 and p=0.41), indicating the effect is specific to forebrain regions (pallium/subpallium) rather than a global brain phenomenon.

result: By 9 dpf, movement restraint reduced forebrain size and, after correcting for size, still significantly reduced the proportion of PCNA+ cells and tbr2+ intermediate progenitors in the forebrain, without affecting GFAP+ radial neural stem cells.
evaluation: Claims C14-C17 show that prolonged restraint affects both brain size and the proliferative cell population. The statistical evidence is strong (p<0.01 for PCNA+ and tbr2+ cells), and the lack of effect on GFAP+ stem cells suggests the impact is on progenitor proliferation/differentiation rather than stem cell depletion.

result: Movement restraint increased the proportion of newly generated cells (EdU+) that co-labeled with the neuronal marker Elavl3 in both pallium and subpallium without affecting the absolute number of EdU+ cells produced, suggesting movement regulates progenitor self-renewal versus differentiation rather than cell cycle length.
evaluation: Claims C19-C22 and C80 provide strong evidence for the mechanism: movement restraint biases cells toward differentiation over self-renewal. Statistical support is robust (p<0.01 for pallium, p=0.01 for subpallium), and the lack of change in absolute EdU+ cell numbers (p>0.4) supports the interpretation that cell fate decisions, not proliferation rate, are affected.

result: Movement restraint did not affect apoptosis (activated caspase-3+ cells) in the forebrain by 6 dpf but significantly increased apoptosis specifically in the pallium (not subpallium) by 9 dpf.
evaluation: Claims C23-C26 demonstrate that apoptosis is not the primary mechanism for reduced proliferative cells at 6 dpf (p=0.32), but becomes a contributing factor by 9 dpf (p<0.01 in pallium). The regional specificity (pallium but not subpallium) is well-documented, though apoptosis rates remain relatively low overall.

result: Larvae reared against a strong water current exhibited a greater proportion of PCNA+ cells specifically in the pallium (not subpallium) at both 6 and 9 dpf, without affecting brain region size.
evaluation: Claims C27-C31 demonstrate the opposite effect of restraint: increased movement increases pallial proliferation. Statistical support is provided (p=0.01 at 9 dpf, p=0.03 at 6 dpf for pallium; p>0.2 for subpallium), confirming the bidirectional and region-specific relationship between movement and neurogenesis.

result: Rearing larvae against a current reduced the proportion of newly generated cells expressing Elavl3 and did not affect body length, suggesting increased movement maintains an expanded proliferative population over neuronal differentiation independent of overall growth effects.
evaluation: Claims C32-C33 provide mechanistic insight complementary to the restraint experiments, showing that increased movement promotes progenitor maintenance over differentiation (p=0.04). The lack of body length effect (p=0.51) rules out general growth as a confounding factor.

result: Complete immobilization (blocking tail movement) significantly reduced pallial PCNA+ cells by 6 dpf, while removing visual stimulation alone had no effect. Neither manipulation affected subpallial PCNA+ cells or total cell numbers.
evaluation: Claims C34-C37 isolate physical movement as the critical sensory modality. Statistical support is strong (p<0.01 for tail movement effect, p=0.13 for subpallium), and the specificity to PCNA+ cells without affecting total cell numbers confirms the effect is on proliferation, not general cell survival.

result: Ablation of lateral line hair cells using copper sulfate did not affect pallial PCNA+ cells in unrestrained larvae, indicating the lateral line does not mediate movement-dependent neurogenesis.
evaluation: Claims C38, C82-C83 rule out the lateral line as the sensory mechanism. The experimental approach is well-established (cited to Mackenzie and Raible, 2012), and the lack of effect (p=0.62) is appropriately interpreted as negative evidence for this pathway.

result: AG1478 treatment from 8-30 hpf prevented trunk DRG development without affecting pallium size or PCNA+ cells at 3 dpf or swimming behavior at 6 dpf, but blocked the movement-dependent change in pallial PCNA+ cells observed in DMSO-treated larvae.
evaluation: Claims C39-C41 and C73 establish that DRG-deficient larvae show attenuated neurogenic responses to movement. The experimental design includes appropriate controls (no effect at 3 dpf before movement manipulation, p=0.97; no swimming impairment), and the blocking of movement-dependent effects (p<0.01) implicates DRG in the pathway.

result: AG1478-treated larvae showed effects on pallial neurogenesis similar to movement restraint (increased Elavl3/EdU co-labeling, reduced PCNA+ cells), and by 9 dpf exhibited attenuated movement-dependent differences in pallial PCNA+ cells compared to DMSO controls, despite normal swimming behavior.
evaluation: Claims C42-C44, C75-C76 demonstrate that DRG deficiency mimics some restraint effects and attenuates movement-dependent neurogenesis. Statistical support is provided (p=0.04 for Elavl3/EdU, p<0.01 for 9 dpf effects), though the partial rather than complete blocking suggests other pathways may also contribute.

result: Photoactivation of TRPA1 receptors in DRG using Optovin and light in immobilized larvae produced repeatable motor responses and significantly increased pallial PCNA+ cells, while DMSO-treated controls showed no such responses or neurogenic effects.
evaluation: Claims C45-C49 and C77-C79 provide strong evidence that DRG activation is sufficient to drive pallial neurogenesis even without physical movement. The optopharmacological approach is well-established (cited to Kokel et al., 2013; Prober et al., 2008), statistical support is adequate (p<0.01 for motor responses, p=0.04 for PCNA+ increase), and appropriate controls are included.

result: DRG-deficient larvae (AG1478-treated) did not exhibit the Optovin-and-light-dependent increase in pallial PCNA+ cells observed in control larvae.
evaluation: Claim C50 provides critical evidence that the Optovin effect requires DRG, confirming DRG as the cellular target. Statistical support is provided (p=0.04), and this result completes the causal chain linking DRG activation to pallial neurogenesis.

result: Movement maintains an expanded pool of forebrain neural precursors by promoting progenitor self-renewal over neuronal production, and this effect is mediated by dorsal root ganglia (DRG), as evidenced by attenuated responses in DRG-deficient larvae and increased proliferation following targeted DRG photoactivation in immobilized larvae.
evaluation: Claims C53-C56 represent the main conclusions synthesized from the experimental findings. These summary claims are well-supported by the collective evidence from restraint, exercise, immobilization, DRG ablation, and optogenetic experiments presented throughout the manuscript.

result: tbr2 is a protein marker of intermediate progenitors and newly generated neurons.
evaluation: Claim C18 is a well-established fact in the field, supported by citation to Englund et al., 2005. This marker characterization is standard and appropriately applied in the study.

result: Dorsal root ganglia (DRG) are sensory neurons that convey mechanical sensations from the zebrafish trunk and communicate signals via ascending pathways to the CNS in the spinal cord.
evaluation: Claims C69 and C84 describe established knowledge about DRG function, supported by citation to Vandewauw et al., 2013. This background information appropriately contextualizes the experimental work.

result: Movement-dependent maintenance of the progenitor pool may involve the Shh signaling pathway, which expands progenitor populations via symmetric cell division.
evaluation: Claim C81 is speculative and not directly tested in this study. While the citations (Lai et al., 2003; Machold et al., 2003; Yang et al., 2015) support the role of Shh in progenitor expansion, no experiments in this manuscript examine Shh signaling. This represents a plausible hypothesis for future work rather than a supported result.

result: AG1478 treatment blocks trunk DRG development but not head DRG populations derived from neural crest cells, and previous studies have shown AG1478 can impair embryonic proliferation in the optic tectum at higher concentrations.
evaluation: Claims C85-C86 provide important context about the AG1478 treatment, supported by citations to Honjo et al., 2008 and Sato et al., 2015. The authors appropriately acknowledge potential limitations and address them through control experiments showing no effect at 3 dpf.

result: Rohon-Beard cells were originally thought to die off entirely by 4 dpf, but subsequent work suggests they may persist up to 1-2 weeks post-fertilization.
evaluation: Claims C87-C88 accurately represent evolving understanding in the field, supported by appropriate citations (Reyes et al., 2004; Kucenas et al., 2006; Palanca et al., 2013). This context is relevant for interpreting the DRG experiments.

result: TRPA1 channels are evolutionarily conserved across vertebrates and have been implicated in touch stimuli in DRG and sensory neurons, as well as in transducing chemosensory and nociceptive input.
evaluation: Claims C89-C92 provide appropriate background on TRPA1 function, well-supported by multiple citations (Christensen and Corey, 2007; Kwan et al., 2006; Brierley et al., 2011; Kindt et al., 2007; Prober et al., 2008). This contextualizes the use of Optovin for DRG activation.

result: The postembryonic brain exhibits experience-dependent development with elevated neuroplasticity, traditionally thought to occur through changes in pre-existing neurons, though neurogenesis persists postembryonically and may be regulated by sensory experience.
evaluation: Claims C51-C52, C57-C61 establish the scientific context and rationale for the study. These are well-supported by appropriate citations (Knudsen, 2004; Lindsey and Tropepe, 2006; Wei et al., 2011; He et al., 2014) and represent established knowledge in the field.

result: Exercise-induced neurogenesis in the adult mammalian hippocampus is a well-characterized model that has been linked to improvements in spatial learning, cognitive flexibility, and has been incorporated as a therapeutic intervention for neuropsychiatric disorders.
evaluation: Claims C62-C65 provide important comparative context from the mammalian literature, well-supported by citations (van Praag et al., 1999a,b; Anacker and Hen, 2017; Vakhrusheva et al., 2016; Kandola et al., 2016). This establishes the broader significance of the zebrafish findings.

result: Physical activity correlates with cognitive function in human children, motor development begins early postembryonically across vertebrates, and if the movement-neurogenesis relationship is conserved, it may help explain correlations between physical and mental development, including comorbidity of impairments and associations between sedentary lifestyle and depression.
evaluation: Claims C66, C93-C97 extend the findings to broader implications for human development. While the citations support the correlations described (Tomporowski et al., 2008; Best, 2010; de Vries et al., 1982; Barnett et al., 2012; Anton et al., 2006; Jacobs et al., 2000), the connection to the zebrafish findings is speculative. The conservation of this mechanism across taxa remains to be demonstrated.

result: Larval zebrafish first begin to exhibit voluntary movements during the developmental period studied and continue to exhibit elevated rates of neurogenesis in many brain divisions compared to adulthood.
evaluation: Claims C67-C68 justify the choice of developmental stage for the study, supported by appropriate citations (Buss and Drapeau, 2001; Lindsey and Tropepe, 2006; Feliciano et al., 2015). This establishes the suitability of the model system.
